1.explanation: The Ruby language definition in src/languages/ruby.js is where highlight.js defines the patterns for here-documents. The mode’s regex for recognizing the start and end of a heredoc doesn’t account for the quoted tag syntax (<<-'TAG'). As a result, non-interpolated heredocs (which require a quoted delimiter) aren’t parsed as strings. Updating the regex and mode logic in this file to allow quoted identifiers (single- and double-quoted) will fix the highlighting for <<-'TAG' blocks.
1.bug_scenario: When using Ruby’s non-interpolated heredoc syntax (the variant that begins with <<-'TAG' and ends with TAG), highlight.js’s Ruby highlighter fails to treat the entire block as a string. After the opening delimiter (which includes a single-quoted tag), string highlighting stops and the closing delimiter isn’t recognized, so the content and terminator are shown as plain code rather than part of a here-document string.

2.explanation: The only place the heredoc patterns for Ruby are defined is in src/languages/ruby.js. That file’s `begin` and `end` regexes for HEREDOCs recognize unquoted and double-quoted delimiters but omit support for single-quoted delimiters (<<-'DELIM'). As a result, single-quoted heredocs never match the closing delimiter. Fixing the regex in ruby.js to allow an optional single quote around the delimiter will correct the highlighting.
2.bug_scenario: In the Ruby mode, standard (interpolated) HEREDOCs like <<-MESSAGE…MESSAGE are recognized and fully highlighted as strings. However, single-quoted heredocs (<<-'MESSAGE'…MESSAGE) are not treated as string blocks—only the opening delimiter is picked up as a string and the highlighter never sees the closing delimiter, so the remainder of the file is colored as if it were inside the string.
